Conservation laws for the Kudryashov-Sinelshchikov equation of second order

Yuri Dimitrov Bozhkov Affiliation: Instituto de Matemática, Estatística e Computação Científica–IMECC, Affiliation: Universidade Estadual de Campinas – UNICAMP Affiliation: Rua Sérgio Buarque de Holanda, 651, 1308313083-859859 - Campinas - SP, Brasil, Email: bozhkov@ime.unicamp.br    Stylianos Dimas Affiliation: Departamento de Matemática, Affiliation: Instituto Tecnológico da Aeronáutica - ITA, Affiliation: Praça Marechal Eduardo Gomes, 50, Vila das Acácias, Affiliation: 12228−90012228-900 - São Jose dos Campos - SP, Brasil, Email: sdimas@ita.br    Oscar Mario Londoño Duque Affiliation: Instituto de Matemática, Estatística e Computação Científica–IMECC, Affiliation: Universidade Estadual de Campinas – UNICAMP Affiliation: Rua Sérgio Buarque de Holanda, 651, 1308313083-859859 - Campinas - SP, Brasil, Affiliation: olondon2@hotmail.com, ra154278@ime.unicamp.br
19 April 2019

Abstract: We establish conservation laws for the second order Kudryashov– Sinelshchikov equation, which models pressure waves in liquid with bubbles. For this purpose we use the method of Nail Ibragimov based on the notion of nonlinear self-adjointness.

Key-words: Lie point symmetries; Nonlinear self-adjointness; Conservations laws; Nail Ibragimov’s method.

This paper is dedicated to Professor Nail Ibragimov in Memoriam

1 Introduction

In [12], Kudryashov and Sinelshchikov studied nonlinear pressure waves in a mixture of a liquid and gas bubbles. Among other results and considerations, they obtained the following second order partial differential equation:

ut+u​ux−(1+u)​ux​x−ux2=0.u_{t}+uu_{x}-(1+u)u_{xx}-u_{x}^{2}=0. (1)

Here tt and xx are the independent variables and u=u⁡(t,x)u=u(t,x) denotes the dimensionless dependent variable. We shall call the Eq. (1)(\ref{eqq1}) the Kudryashov-Sinelshchikov equation.

The purpose of this paper is to establish nontrivial conservation laws by using the N. Ibragimov’s conservation theorem [8, 9, 10, 11], which is done in section 3. For this aim we first study in section 2 the nonlinear self-adjointness of the more general class of partial differential equations

ut−f⁡(u)​ux−g⁡(u)​ux​x+h⁡(u)​ux2=0,u_{t}-f(u)u_{x}-g(u)u_{xx}+h(u)u_{x}^{2}=0, (2)

where the functions f,g,hf,g,h satisfy the conditions

f≠0,g≠0,g′≠0,f\neq 0,\;g\neq 0,\;g^{\prime}\neq 0, (3)

and ′ denotes the derivative d/d​ud/du.

We suppose that the reader is familiar with the basic concepts of Lie point symmetries of differential equations. The fundamental monographs in this area are [1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 13, 14] .

2 Nonlinear Self-Adjointness

We first briefly present the main definitions in the N. Ibragimov’s approach to nonlinear self-adjointness of differential equations adopted to our specific case. For further details the interested reader is directed to [11, 10, 9, 8, 5].

Consider an s−s-th order evolution equation

𝔉⁡(t,x,u(1),u(2),⋯,u(s))=0\mathfrak{F}(t,x,u_{(1)},u_{(2)},\cdots,u_{(s)})=0 (4)

with independent variables t,xt,x and a dependent variable uu, where u(1),u(2)u_{(1)},u_{(2)},.
..u(s)u_{(s)} denote the collection of 1,2,…,s−1,2,...,s-th order partial derivatives of uu.

Definition 2.1.

Let 𝔉\mathfrak{F} be a differential function and ν=ν⁡(t,x)−\nu=\nu(t,x)-the new dependent variable, known as the adjoint variable or nonlocal variable [11]. The formal Lagrangian for 𝔉=0\mathfrak{F}=0 is the differential function defined by

𝔏:=ν​𝔉.\mathfrak{L}:=\nu\mathfrak{F}. (5)
Definition 2.2.

Let 𝔉\mathfrak{F} be a differential function and for the differential equation (4), denoted by 𝔉⁡[u]=0\mathfrak{F}[u]=0, we define the adjoint differential function to 𝔉\mathfrak{F} by

𝔉∗:=δ​𝔏δ​u\mathfrak{F}^{*}:=\frac{\delta\mathfrak{L}}{\delta u} (6)

and the adjoint differential equation by

𝔉∗​[u,ν]=0,\mathfrak{F}^{*}[u,\nu]=0, (7)

where the Euler operator

δδ​u=∂∂u+∑m=1∞Dxi1⋯Dxim∂∂uxi1xi2⋯xim\frac{\delta}{\delta u}=\frac{\partial}{\partial u}+\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}D_{x_{i_{1}}}\cdots D_{x_{i_{m}}}\frac{\partial}{\partial{u_{x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\cdots x_{i_{m}}}}} (8)

and DxiD_{x_{i}}is the total derivative operator with respect to xix_{i} defined by

Dxi=∂xi+uxi∂u+uxi​xj∂uxj+⋯+uxixi1xi2⋯xin∂uxi1xi2⋯xin…D_{x_{i}}=\partial_{x_{i}}+u_{x_{i}}\partial_{u}+u_{x_{i}x_{j}}\partial_{u_{x_{j}}}+\cdots+u_{x_{i}x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\cdots x_{i_{n}}}\partial_{u_{x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\cdots x_{i_{n}}}}...
Definition 2.3.

The differential equation (4) is said to be nonlinearly self-adjoint if there exists a substitution

ν=ϕ⁡(t,x,u)≠0\nu=\phi(t,x,u)\neq 0 (9)

such that

𝔉∗∣ν=ϕ⁡(t,x,u)=λ​𝔉\mathfrak{F}^{*}\mid_{\nu=\phi(t,x,u)}=\lambda\mathfrak{F} (10)

for some undetermined coefficient λ=λ⁡(t,x,u,⋯).\lambda=\lambda(t,x,u,\cdots). If ν=ϕ⁡(u)\nu=\phi(u) in (9) and (10), the equation (4) is called quasi self-adjoint. If ν=u\nu=u, we say that the equation (4) is strictly self-adjoint.

Now we shall obtain the adjoint equation to the eq. (2). For this purpose we write (2) in the form (4), where

𝔉:=ut−f⁡(u)​ux−g⁡(u)​ux​x+h⁡(u)​ux2=0.\mathfrak{F}:=u_{t}-f(u)u_{x}-g(u)u_{xx}+h(u)u_{x}^{2}=0. (11)

Then the corresponding formal Lagrangian (5) is given by

𝔏:=ν⁡(ut−f⁡(u)​ux−g⁡(u)​ux​x+h⁡(u)​ux2)=0\mathfrak{L}:=\nu(u_{t}-f(u)u_{x}-g(u)u_{xx}+h(u)u_{x}^{2})=0 (12)

and the Euler operator (8) assumes the following form:

δ​𝔏δ​u=∂𝔏∂u−Dt​∂𝔏∂ut−Dx​∂𝔏∂ux+Dx2​∂𝔏∂ux​x.\frac{\delta\mathfrak{L}}{\delta u}=\frac{\partial\mathfrak{L}}{\partial u}-D_{t}\frac{\partial\mathfrak{L}}{\partial{u_{t}}}-D_{x}\frac{\partial\mathfrak{L}}{\partial{u_{x}}}+D_{x}^{2}\frac{\partial\mathfrak{L}}{\partial{u_{xx}}}. (13)

We calculate explicitly the Euler operator (13) applied to 𝔏\mathfrak{L} determined by (12). In this way we obtain the adjoint equation (7) to (2):

𝔉∗\displaystyle\mathfrak{F}^{*} =\displaystyle= −νt+f⁡(u)​νx−g⁡(u)​νx​x−2​ν​g′​(u)​ux​x−2​ν​h​(u)​ux​x\displaystyle-\nu_{t}+f(u)\nu_{x}-g(u)\nu_{xx}-2\nu g^{\prime}(u)u_{xx}-2\nu h(u)u_{xx} (14)
−\displaystyle- ν​h′​(u)​ux2−ν​g′′​(u)​ux2−2​g′​(u)​νx​ux−2​h​(u)​ux​νx=0.\displaystyle\nu h^{\prime}(u)u_{x}^{2}-\nu g^{\prime\prime}(u)u_{x}^{2}-2g^{\prime}(u)\nu_{x}u_{x}-2h(u)u_{x}\nu_{x}=0.

The main result in this section can be stated as follows.

Theorem 1.

The generalized Kudryashov-Sinelshchikov equation (2)(\ref{eq1}) is nonlinearly self-adjoint.

If f⁡(u)=a​g​(u)+bf(u)=ag(u)+b, a,b−a,b-constants, and f⁡(u)f(u) itself is not a constant, then the substitution is given by

ϕ(t,x,u)=(c1exp(ax+abt)+c2)exp(−∫g′​(u)+h​(u)g⁡(u)du).\phi(t,x,u)=(c_{1}\exp(ax+abt)+c_{2})\exp\left({\displaystyle{-\int{\frac{g^{\prime}(u)+h(u)}{g(u)}du}}}\right). (15)

If f⁡(u)=b−f(u)=b-constant, then the corresponding substitution is given by

ϕ(t,x,u)=(c3(x+bt)+c4)exp(−∫g′​(u)+h​(u)g⁡(u)du).\phi(t,x,u)=(c_{3}(x+bt)+c_{4})\exp\left({\displaystyle{-\int{\frac{g^{\prime}(u)+h(u)}{g(u)}du}}}\right). (16)

In the rest of the cases, the substitution is

ϕ(u)=c5exp(−∫g′​(u)+h​(u)g⁡(u)du).\displaystyle\phi(u)=c_{5}\exp\left({\displaystyle{-\int{\frac{g^{\prime}(u)+h(u)}{g(u)}du}}}\right). (17)

The constants c1,c2,c3,c4,c5c_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4},c_{5} are such that (c1,c2)≠(0,0)(c_{1},c_{2})\neq(0,0), (c3,c4)≠(0,0)(c_{3},c_{4})\neq(0,0) and c5≠0c_{5}\neq 0.

Proof.

Substituting in (14), and then in (10), ν=ϕ⁡(t,x,u)\nu=\phi(t,x,u) and its respective partial derivatives, and comparing the corresponding coefficients we get four equations:

g⁡(u)​ϕu+(h⁡(u)+g′​(u))​ϕ=0,g(u)\phi_{u}+(h(u)+g^{\prime}(u))\phi=0, (18)
g⁡(u)​ϕu​u+(h⁡(u)+2​g′​(u))​ϕu+(h′​(u)+g′′​(u))​ϕ=0.g(u)\phi_{uu}+(h(u)+2g^{\prime}(u))\phi_{u}+(h^{\prime}(u)+g^{\prime\prime}(u))\phi=0. (19)
g⁡(u)​ϕx​u+(h⁡(u)+g′​(u))​ϕx=0,g(u)\phi_{xu}+(h(u)+g^{\prime}(u))\phi_{x}=0, (20)
OPENϕt−f⁡(u)​ϕx+g⁡(u))​ϕx​x=0\phi_{t}-f(u)\phi_{x}+g(u))\phi_{xx}=0 (21)

We observe that Eq.(19) is obtaned from Eq.(18) by differentiation with respect to uu as well as that Eq.(20) is obtaned from Eq.(18) by differentiation with respect to xx. Therefore we have to study only Eqs. (18) and (21).

Solving for ϕ\phi in (18) we obtain

ϕ(t,x,u)=M(t,x)exp(−∫g′​(u)+h​(u)g⁡(u)du)\phi(t,x,u)=M(t,x)\exp\left({\displaystyle{-\int{\frac{g^{\prime}(u)+h(u)}{g(u)}du}}}\right) (22)

for certain function M⁡(t,x)M(t,x). Substituting (22) into (21) we get that

Mt−f⁡(u)​Mx+g⁡(u)​Mx​x=0.M_{t}-f(u)M_{x}+g(u)M_{xx}=0. (23)

Consider now the Wronskian

W=W⁡(1,−f,g)=f′′​g′−f′​g′′.W=W(1,-f,g)=f^{\prime\prime}g^{\prime}-f^{\prime}g^{\prime\prime}.

1.) If W≠0W\neq 0 then Mt=Mx=0M_{t}=M_{x}=0 from (23). Hence M=M=const., and in this case the equation is quasi self-adjoint.

2.) Let W=0W=0. Since g′≠0g^{\prime}\neq 0 (see (3)) we divide by g′2g^{\prime 2} and obtain

(f′​(u)g′​(u))′=0.\left(\frac{f^{\prime}(u)}{g^{\prime}(u)}\right)^{\prime}=0.

Thus f′=a​g′f^{\prime}=ag^{\prime} and f⁡(u)=a​g​(u)+bf(u)=ag(u)+b, with a,b−a,b-constants.

Let a≠0a\neq 0. We note that this condition is equivalent to the fact that the function f⁡(u)f(u) is not a constant.

We substitute this form of ff into (23):

Mt−b​Mx+g⁡(u)​(Mx​x−a​Mx)=0.M_{t}-bM_{x}+g(u)(M_{xx}-aM_{x})=0. (24)

Differentiating (24) with respect to uu we obtain that (Mx​x−a​Mx)​g′​(u)=0(M_{xx}-aM_{x})g^{\prime}(u)=0. Hence

Mx​x−a​Mx=0M_{xx}-aM_{x}=0 (25)

since g′≠0g^{\prime}\neq 0. Further we substitute the general solution

M⁡(t,x)=c1​(t)​exp⁡(a​x)+c2​(t)M(t,x)=c_{1}(t)\exp(ax)+c_{2}(t)

of the last equation into Mt−b​Mx=0M_{t}-bM_{x}=0 (see (24)), and obtain that

M⁡(t,x)=c1​exp⁡(a​x+a​b​t)+c2,M(t,x)=c_{1}\exp(ax+abt)+c_{2},

where c1,c2c_{1},c_{2} are arbitrary constants and a≠0a\neq 0.

If a=0a=0 then f⁡(u)=b−f(u)=b-constant and Mx​x=0M_{xx}=0 from (25). Therefore M⁡(t,x)=c3​(t)​x+c4​(t)M(t,x)=c_{3}(t)x+c_{4}(t). Substituting this into Mt−b​Mx=0M_{t}-bM_{x}=0 we finally obtain that M⁡(t,x)=c3​(x+b​t)+c4M(t,x)=c_{3}(x+bt)+c_{4}, where c3,c4c_{3},c_{4} are arbitrary constants. ∎

Observation. The equations (18)–(21) can be directly obtained from [4].

This theorem has some immedate consequences.

Corollary 1.1.

The generalized Kudryashov-Sinelshchikov equation (2)(\ref{eq1}) is quasi self-adjoint with the substitution

ϕ(u)=Mexp(−∫g′​(u)+h​(u)g⁡(u)du)\displaystyle\phi(u)=M\exp\left({\displaystyle{-\int{\frac{g^{\prime}(u)+h(u)}{g(u)}du}}}\right) (26)

where M≠0M\neq 0 is a constant.

Corollary 1.2.

The generalized Kudryashov-Sinelshchikov equation (2)(\ref{eq1}) is strictly self-adjoint if and only if

h⁡(u)=−g⁡(u)u−g′​(u).\displaystyle h(u)=-\frac{g(u)}{u}-g^{\prime}(u). (27)
Corollary 1.3.

The Kudryashov-Sinelshchikov equation (1)(\ref{eqq1}) is nonlinearly self-adjoint with the substitution

ϕ⁡(u)=c1​exp⁡(−t−x)+c2\displaystyle\phi(u)=c_{1}\exp(-t-x)+c_{2} (28)

with (c1,c2)≠(0,0)−(c_{1},c_{2})\neq(0,0)-constants. It is not strictly self-adjoint equation.

The results in this section are compatible with the considerations of N. Ibragimov, [11], pp. 20–21, on the self-adjointnes of the nonlinear heat equation.

3 Conservation laws

Following the classical S. Lie algorithm it is easy to obtain that the Lie point symmetries of equation (1) are determined by the vector fields

X1=∂t,X2=∂x,X3=t∂t−t∂x−(1+u)∂u.X_{1}=\partial_{t},\;\;X_{2}=\partial_{x},\;\;X_{3}=t\partial_{t}-t\partial_{x}-(1+u)\partial_{u}. (29)

In this section we shall establish some conservation laws for the Kudrya-shov-Sinelshchikov equation (1) using the conservation theorem of N. Ibra-gimov in [11].

To begin with, we observe that Eq. (1) itself is a conservation laws since it can be written in the form

Dt​u+Dx​[u2/2−(1+u)​ux]=0.D_{t}u+D_{x}[u^{2}/2-(1+u)u_{x}]=0. (30)

Since the Eq. (1) is of second order, the formal Lagrangian contains derivatives up to order two. Thus, the general formula in [11] for the components of the conserved vector is reduced to

Ci\displaystyle C^{i} =\displaystyle= W⁡[∂𝔏∂ui−Dj​(∂𝔏∂ui​j)]+Dj​[W]​[∂𝔏∂ui​j],\displaystyle W\left[\frac{\partial\mathfrak{L}}{\partial_{u_{i}}}-D_{j}(\frac{\partial\mathfrak{L}}{\partial_{u_{ij}}})\right]+D_{j}[W]\left[\frac{\partial\mathfrak{L}}{\partial_{u_{ij}}}\right], (31)

where

W=η−ξj​uj,W=\eta-{\xi}^{j}u_{j},

i,j=1,2i,j=1,2, the formal Lagrangian

𝔏=ν⁡(ut+u​ux−(1+u)​ux​x−ux2)\mathfrak{L}=\nu(u_{t}+uu_{x}-(1+u)u_{xx}-u_{x}^{2})

and ξ1,ξ2,η{\xi}^{1},{\xi}^{2},\eta are the infinitesimals of a Lie point symmetry admitted by Eq. (1), given in (29).

If c1=0c_{1}=0 in the substitution (28), then the resulting conservation laws are trivial. Therefore we can set c1=1c_{1}=1 and c2=0c_{2}=0 without loss of generality. Hence

ν=exp⁡(−t−x).\nu=\exp(-t-x).

Using (1) and (31) we obtain that the symmetry X2X_{2} determines the following conserved vector C=(C1,C2)C=(C^{1},C^{2}), where

C1=−ux​exp⁡(−t−x),C2=(ut+(1+u)​ux)​exp⁡(−t−x).C^{1}=-u_{x}\exp(-t-x),\;\;\;C^{2}=(u_{t}+(1+u)u_{x})\exp(-t-x).

Similarly, for X1X_{1} we get

C1=−utexp(−t−x),C2=[ut(1+ux)+(1+u)ut​x)exp(−t−x).C^{1}=-u_{t}\exp(-t-x),\;\;\;C^{2}=[u_{t}(1+u_{x})+(1+u)u_{tx})\exp(-t-x).

Further, we apply the simplifying procedure of transfering terms of form Dx​(…)D_{x}(...) from C1C^{1} to C2C^{2}, described on pp. 50–51 of [11], in order to eliminate the second partial derivatives of uu. After some work, the components of the conserved vector C=(C1,C2)C=(C^{1},C^{2}) become

C1=[u2/2−(1+u)​ux]​exp⁡(−t−x),C^{1}=[u^{2}/2-(1+u)u_{x}]\exp(-t-x),
C2=[−u2/2+(1+u)ut+(1+u)ux]exp(−t−x).C^{2}=[-u^{2}/2+(1+u)u_{t}+(1+u)u_{x}]\exp(-t-x).

Analogously, for the symmetry X3X_{3} we obtain conserved vector C=(C1,C2)C=(C^{1},C^{2}) with

C1=[−(1+u)+t​u2/2−t​u​ux]​exp⁡(−t−x),C^{1}=[-(1+u)+tu^{2}/2-tuu_{x}]\exp(-t-x),
C2=[(1+u)+(1+u)​ux+u2/2+t​u​ut−t​u2/2]​exp⁡(−t−x).C^{2}=[(1+u)+(1+u)u_{x}+u^{2}/2+tuu_{t}-tu^{2}/2]\exp(-t-x).
